items.title: OpenAI bots meddled with multiple US government agency sites
items.summary: OpenAI said its bots accessed public data from a range of institutions during test exercises.
items.content:
OpenAI has acknowledged that it alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been meddled with by its AI bots acting improperly.

AI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions", including the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Census Bureau and Education Department, the company said.

The disclosures come days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that OpenAI agents had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme.

Since August, public fears have grown over the potentially serious, even life-threatening, impacts of AI tools falling outside of human control.

OpenAI said that some of the data was accessed by AI agents, essentially bots that are designed and trained to operate somewhat autonomously, which were working to find "authoritative sources of public information".

But the company noted that some of the bots went beyond that and worked to bypass security measures on websites.

When attempting to get information from the Census Bureau, for instance, AI agents used tools reserved for software developers to access it, the company said.

OpenAI said all of the government data accessed by bots was public.

However, it noted that information that its bots accessed from the SEC, which regulates the US stock market and protects investors, was later published by AI agents on another website. OpenAI says this action was not intended.

In other instances that OpenAI disclosed on Friday, its AI agents transferred data when it should not have.

Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.

The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had opted in to allow OpenAI to train models using their data.

Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted: "This is not an appropriate use of this data."

It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.

Reuters first reported the expanded investigations. OpenAI also published details to its public blog.

In certain instances of the agent activity, OpenAI said the tools "bypassed" security controls of some websites.

In other instances, the AI agents showed "misalignment" in attempts to get at information from websites. Misalignment is a term used by AI companies and researchers to describe instances where an AI tool did something that it was not trained to do or was otherwise unintended.

OpenAI said that it was limiting identifying what entities were impacted because many had asked the company to not disclose details.

"Our goal is to give each organization the facts and defer to them on if and when to make the incident public," it said.

Not all of the instances involved in this incident were being considered a significant security breach, the company noted.

"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning," it explained. "Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address."

Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?

The company said many of the incidents are being referred to as "agent spam", which it described as "unexpected or concerning" AI agent activity, like posting information to the internet.

OpenAI began taking such incidents more seriously after an incident in July where a group, or "swarm," of its AI agents hacked the AI developer platform Hugging Face without being prompted to do so.

Hugging Face was first to go public with the incident, with OpenAI publicly taking responsibility for it later.

Clement Delangue, the head of Hugging Face, during a United Nations Security Council session on AI on Wednesday: "I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to disclose this attack publicly."

"Especially now that we know similar incidents had been happening months earlier in secret at a handful of frontier labs without monitoring," Delangue added.

During that same UN meeting, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, the head of rival firm Anthropic, asked for international leaders to form global standards for AI safety and ways to monitor and report such incidents.

While OpenAI and Anthropic have both said in recent weeks that they will bring third-party evaluators inside their companies to do real-time safety evaluations of AI tools and models, such evaluators have not yet arrived, as the BBC has reported .

OpenAI said on Friday that it is currently reviewing training activity by its AI agents and going back on a "month by month" basis from when the Hugging Face hack occurred.

"Most cases identified so far have been low severity, with limited or no evidence of meaningful impact," the company said. "Given the scale of the review required, and the need to verify each case, this work will take months to complete."

David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at University of Montreal and the founder of AI safety group Evitable, said on Friday that he was "deeply troubled" by the increasing number of AI-related safety incidents.

He called for "an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium" on AI development.

"We have yet to understand the extent of existing incidents, and future rogue AI scenarios could be catastrophic," Krueger said.

items.title: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged', police say
items.summary: Tasia Fortune's body was found hanging from a tree on the grounds of an abandoned home in Jackson in August.
items.content:
Police in the US state of Mississippi have said that they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" and placed hanging in a tree.

The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune, a mother of four, had been killed in a dispute related to drugs.

The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests.

In a news release, police said that the medical examiner had determined that Fortune's death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".

Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging was staged.

Fortune's mother told the BBC that she remembers the coroner telling her: "we're not treating this as [an] actual hanging." Her daughter, they told her, was dead before being placed in the tree.

Christy Spivey also recalled police telling her the incident was "drug related".

Speaking to reporters outside the Jackson Police Department on Friday, Spivey described how she knows her daughter fought for her life till the very end.

"I know she did. I know my daughter," Spivey told reporters. Fortune leaves behind four young children, ages 7, 5, 4 and 1, she added.

Dressed in a shirt that reads "Justice for Tasia Fortune", Spivey stressed that she does not want to see any innocent people going to jail.

Three people have so far been arrested in relation to the case, all of whom are black, including Jarques Ratliff, 51, who has pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody without bond.

A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in the case this week.

A third, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder. He is scheduled to appear in court on Monday.

The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country.

Representative Ayanna Pressley, Democrat of Massachusetts, cites at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress , external , which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers.

The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has been ruled a suicide.

Arrest made over the death of black woman found hanged from tree in Mississippi

Mother demands answers, weeks after black woman found hanging from Mississippi tree

items.title: IA da 120 miliardi di parametri anche senza cloud. Il segreto è MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+
items.summary: Un sistema desktop compatto da 4 litri offre memoria unificata ad alta capacità, inferenza privata sul dispositivo e scalabilità multisistema per i flussi di lavoro professionali basati sull'intelligenza artificiale ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
L'intelligenza artificiale sta diventando parte integrante del lavoro quotidiano, ma non tutte le organizzazioni desiderano che ogni richiesta, documento o set di dati venga inviato al cloud. Per i team che lavorano con contratti riservati, banche dati proprietarie, risorse creative o analisi interne, l'IA locale può offrire un accesso più rapido, un maggiore controllo sul luogo in cui vengono elaborati i dati e una minore dipendenza dalla connessione a Internet o dai servizi cloud a consumo.

L'MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ è un desktop compatto con IA edge progettato per questo svolgimento. Costruito su una familiare architettura PC x86, il sistema combina fino a un processore AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, fino a 128GB di memoria unificata LPDDR5X e grafica Radeon 8060S integrata in un telaio in alluminio da 4 litri.

Molti PC compatti sono ottimizzati per carichi di lavoro standard per ufficio. Il PRO MAX EDGE AI+ è costruito attorno a un requisito diverso: fornire alle applicazioni di IA locali accesso a un calcolo e memoria consistenti senza dover utilizzare un PC di grandi dimensioni o una scheda grafica separata.

La configurazione di punta AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 include 16 core Zen 5 CPU, 40 unità di calcolo grafica RDNA™ 3.5 e una NPU XDNA 2 con una potenza fino a 50 TOPS. Su tutta la piattaforma, le prestazioni totali dell'IA raggiungono fino a 126 TOPS. Questa combinazione consente al software compatibile di utilizzare CPU, GPU o NPU a seconda del carico di lavoro, dalla produttività assistita dall'IA all'inferenza locale, al rendering e alla creazione di contenuti.

La capacità di memoria è spesso il fattore limitante quando un computer esegue un grande modello linguistico. Il PRO MAX EDGE AI+ supporta fino a 128GB di memoria unificata LPDDR5X-8000, con fino a 96GB configurabili come memoria grafica.

Invece di separare la memoria di sistema e la memoria grafica fissa in pool isolati, il design unificato permette alle applicazioni compatibili di utilizzare una risorsa condivisa più ampia.

MSI afferma che le configurazioni supportate possono eseguire grandi modelli linguistici con fino a 120 miliardi di parametri sul dispositivo. I test del prodotto MSI mostrano anche che GPT-OSS 120B ha utilizzato circa 65GB di memoria grafica. La dimensione del modello da sola non determina velocità o compatibilità: architettura del modello, quantizzazione, lunghezza del contesto, software, sistema operativo e configurazione della memoria influenzano tutti il risultato reale.

L'esecuzione locale di un carico di lavoro AI compatibile può conservare file e prompt selezionati all'interno dell'ambiente di un'organizzazione. Questo può essere utile per l'analisi privata di documenti, la generazione interna di recupero aumentata (RAG), la ricerca, la prototipazione e la produzione creativa.

L'esecuzione locale può anche ridurre la latenza di rete e mantenere disponibili gli strumenti quando la connettività cloud è limitata. Tuttavia, la privacy dipende ancora dalle applicazioni, dalle impostazioni e dalle politiche di gestione dei dati utilizzate; l'hardware da solo non garantisce un flusso di lavoro sicuro.

Un singolo desktop compatto può essere sufficiente per molte attività di IA locali, ma MSI supporta anche il clustering multi-unità per carichi di lavoro più grandi. La tabella di validazione pubblicata dall'azienda include configurazioni a due nodi per modelli selezionati 120B e 235B e una configurazione a quattro nodi per DeepSeek-V3.1 con 671 miliardi di parametri al Q4_0 quantizzazione.

Per i piccoli team e studi di IA, questo crea un percorso da un desktop a una configurazione di inferenza locale distribuita senza passare immediatamente a un'infrastruttura su scala rack.

L'inferenza AI, il rendering e le operazioni di big data possono imporre una domanda costante su un sistema.

MSI affronta questo problema con raffreddamento Frozr AI Pro, uno spreader di rame, tre heat pipe e un design a tripla ventola. I dissipatori di calore Glacier Armor aggiungono un supporto termico dedicato per i due slot SSD PCIe Gen 4 M.2, aiutando a mantenere le prestazioni di archiviazione durante l'accesso prolungato a file di modello e dataset locali.

Il telaio integra anche l'alimentatore da 300W, quindi non c'è un grande adattatore esterno che occupi spazio sotto la scrivania. Un interruttore fisico a tre stadi consente agli utenti di selezionare profili di alimentazione preimpostati e bilanciare prestazioni, temperatura e acustica senza dover prima navigare in un software utility.

Il PRO MAX EDGE AI+ supporta Wi-Fi 7 e fino a quattro display indipendenti tramite HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4a e due porte USB 40Gbps Type-C con modalità DisplayPort Alt. Fornisce inoltre più porte USB Type-A, connessioni audio anteriori e posteriori, Ethernet RJ45 e un lettore di schede SD 4.0 UHS-II. La combinazione è adatta ad analisi multi-display, montaggi e flussi di lavoro che spostano file di grandi dimensioni tra fotocamere, archiviazione e applicazioni AI locali.

L'MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ è un desktop edge AI da 4 litri per inferenza AI locale, creazione di contenuti, analisi dati e carichi di lavoro aziendali avanzati. È disponibile fino a un processore AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 e fino a 128GB di memoria unificata.

Sì. Modelli e applicazioni AI compatibili possono funzionare localmente sul PRO MAX EDGE AI+. MSI afferma che le configurazioni supportate possono eseguire modelli linguistici con fino a 120 miliardi di parametri sul dispositivo. Compatibilità e prestazioni variano in base al modello, alla quantizzazione, alla lunghezza del contesto, al software e alla configurazione del sistema.

Con un processore AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, la piattaforma offre fino a 126 TOPS di prestazioni totali di intelligenza artificiale. La sua NPU integrata XDNA 2 offre fino a 50 TOPS, oltre a CPU e risorse grafiche Radeon 8060S.

La memoria unificata permette alla CPU e alla GPU integrata di condividere un pool di memoria comune. Il PRO MAX EDGE AI+ supporta fino a 128GB di memoria LPDDR5X, con fino a 96GB assegnabili alla grafica, offrendo ai carichi di lavoro AI compatibili accesso a più memoria grafica rispetto a molti sistemi integrati convenzionali.

Sì. MSI supporta il clustering multi-sistema. La sua validazione pubblicata include modelli selezionati in configurazioni a due e quattro nodi, inclusi DeepSeek-V3.1 671B a quantizzazione Q4_0 su quattro nodi. I risultati dipendono dal modello, dal software e dalla configurazione del cluster.

Il sistema supporta fino a quattro display indipendenti tramite HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4a e due porte USB 40Gbps Type-C con modalità Alt-DisplayPort. Altre connessioni includono USB Type-A, RJ45 Ethernet, jack audio anteriore e posteriore, Wi-Fi 7 e un lettore SD 4.0 UHS-II.

È progettato per sviluppatori di IA, ricercatori, professionisti creativi, piccoli studi e organizzazioni che desiderano un sistema compatto per inferenza locale, flussi di lavoro privati di documenti, creazione di contenuti, analisi o produttività multi-display.

L'MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ sarà disponibile a partire dal mese di ottobre 2026. Configurazioni, disponibilità e prezzi possono variare. Per maggiori informazioni è possibile consultare la pagina prodotto e i canali social ufficiali MSI.

items.title: How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia
items.summary: Exploring the issues behind the escalation of tensions between the TPLF and the national army.
items.content:
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.

Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.

There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.

This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.

It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.

The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.

This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.

This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.

The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.

For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.

It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.

At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.

When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.

Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.

The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.

There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.

The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.

Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.

When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.

The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.

For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.

The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.

But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.

This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.

A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.

Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.

Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.

So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.

TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.

Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.

As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.

It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.

During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.

Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.

Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.

The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.

Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.

This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.

The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.

The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.

It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.

The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.

The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.

The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.

Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.

The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.

The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.

There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.

The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.

The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

items.title: South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
items.summary: Roelf Meyer tells the BBC that being a white Afrikaner gives him legitimacy to challenge Trump's claim of a genocide.
items.content:
South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.

"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.

The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.

Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.

In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.

Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.

Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.

Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.

Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.

"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.

She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".

The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.

In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.

"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."

SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.

Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".

"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.

Race policies or Israel - what's really driving Trump's fury with South Africa?

Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims?

Do Afrikaners want to take Trump up on his South African refugee offer?

An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".

Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.

"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."

Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.

The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.

He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".

"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.

Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.

Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.

While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".

Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".

He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.

The programme has its critics among Afrikaners in South Africa too.

"Why single out the white Afrikaner to say this group qualifies to flee to the US? This country suffers gender-based violence. Why not single out women?" Rudi Swanepoel, a pastor from Johannesburg told the BBC.

Swanepoel thinks it is not persecution but a "loss of privilege" that is causing some Afrikaners to feel aggrieved.

"To use the metaphor of a cake, 30, 40 years ago the white people of South Africa controlled the cake," he says. "Since democracy came, the obvious reality was we had to now start sharing that cake and those privileges."

Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.

Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.

He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.

"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.

But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."

He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.

Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.

"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

items.title: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare
items.summary: Voters are turning away from the centre in Germany as fears grow about the economy and migration.
items.content:
A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His coalition government is in crisis.

But this breakdown of business as usual in Germany has been brewing for years.

It's a nation wrestling with new, uncomfortable and unresolved realities.

Think of certain stereotypes about Germany, and think again.

A country dominated by boring, consensus-driven politics? Not any more.

A confident, powerhouse economy at the cutting edge of car-making? Yesterday's story.

A nation that can be used as a byword for impressive efficiency? The trains don't even run on time.

Many Germans I've spoken to feel their nation has drifted away from the things that once anchored their identity.

That uncertainty is currently embodied by a beleaguered chancellor weakened by bruising regional election results.

In the last fortnight, Friedrich Merz's party was beaten to first place in Berlin, pummelled in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt and pushed out of parliament altogether in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

A lifeline for Merz is that no-one, within his own centre-right CDU party, is yet willing to challenge the chancellor openly despite persistent rumours of a Kanzlertausch (chancellor swap).

But he is on thin ice, with record low approval ratings among voters who often describe him as arrogant and out of touch.

It is a problem that in government circles is sometimes more politely referred to as a "communication" issue.

Those who back the Chancellor say it is time to double down on much-needed reforms, alongside its centre-left SPD coalition partner, and find a better way of talking to people.

Swapping chancellors is not the answer as anyone would face the "same challenges", argues Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy spokesperson in parliament for Merz's CDU and its sister party, the CSU.

Hardt pointed out that the CDU/CSU fared far better in other regional elections earlier this year, when we spoke minutes after Merz addressed party lawmakers at a closed-door meeting in the Bundestag.

"I think Friedrich Merz knows about his deficits," says Hardt. "He will work on him and we will work on us as (a) party. And hopefully we will convince the people in the next months that we are on the right way."

Merz came to power in 2025, promising to get tough on immigration and boost Germany's ailing economy.

He appeared to offer a dynamism that might act as an antidote to the former dull, unhappy drumbeat of centre-left leader Olaf Scholz's bickering three-way coalition.

This week, leading economic institutes raised the country's growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 above 1% while illegal entries into Germany – and Europe – are down year on year.

But that will not eliminate public anxieties, on either issue.

Households and businesses continue to endure high energy costs while fears persist that China is cannibalising German industry, including its iconic car sector.

It is a brutal reversal of Germany's old recipe for success: cheap Russian gas that powered a booming export-driven economy.

And when it comes to immigration, the focus is now less on new arrivals and more on concerns about public safety, welfare costs and integration.

While there are local exceptions, voters appear to be losing faith in Germany's two principal governing parties (CDU and SPD).

Enter the rising force in German politics, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD): a party that alarms security officials with its Russia-friendly stance and contains regional branches that are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence.

Smears and misrepresentations, argues the AfD, as it claimed its third victory ever in a state election last Sunday in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania.

Its co-leader, Alice Weidel, told me this week that Friedrich Merz's days were numbered.

The AfD has survived numerous scandals in recent years to now top the polls nationwide, at around 28%. It carries the swagger of a party making the political weather.

It has capitalised on a nostalgia for the past alongside an anxiety in the present as it consolidates its strongholds in the former communist east.

An AfD placard I saw in Berlin read "Berlin braucht Ordnung" (Berlin needs order). It is the as yet untested promise that this party can bring back a lost sense of stability.

But in Germany's capital it was in fact Die Linke (the Left) that topped the polls last Sunday in a further blow to the country's traditional "big tent" parties.

The victory has put fresh scrutiny on Die Linke, as it faces allegations of antisemitism. The party leadership has insisted it is committed to protecting Jewish life.

This round of regional elections has encapsulated the country's fault lines: the eroding support for Germany's political centre, and a polarising debate on the AfD.

Rarely in post-war Germany has a set of local polls generated so much upheaval at home and interest abroad.

items.title: Inside the FBI hack: Agents fearful and angry after 'dangerous' data breach
items.summary: Current and former agents speak to the BBC about the devastating impact of the FBI hack.
items.content:
Current and former FBI agents have spoken to BBC News of their shock, fear and anger following a hack that appears to have exposed the private and personal information of the agency's entire workforce.

"This is really bad for our undercover agents," says one former FBI agent, who fears for the safety of his colleagues.

The former cyber investigator is in a group chat with current agents who are worried their personal information could soon be freely available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.

He says staff fear they could be targeted, or that criminals could use the data to create highly convincing phishing attempts, scams or demands for bribes.

The hacking group ShinyHunters is threatening to publish the stolen databases and documents within four days unless its demands are met.

Some agents are also concerned about the risk of physical attacks from cyber criminals they have investigated.

"One of the things we are discussing in the group chat is 'violence-as-a-service' attacks from young online gangs," says the former worker .

"They could use this information to harass an FBI agent who has worked on their cases."

Groups similar to ShinyHunters - believed to be an English-speaking gang - have in the past been linked to swatting incidents, and even petrol bomb attacks against law enforcement officers and rivals.

Swatting is a phenomenon so-called because perpetrators make calls that prompt armed police units - called Swat teams in the US - to swoop in on victims.

The group claims it breached FBI systems on Monday and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site.

However, on Wednesday the agency acknowledged the breach - saying it was "aggressively investigating" how it occurred.

For Michael McPherson, a former FBI agent who is now senior vice president of security operations at cyber firm ReliaQuest, the hack presents "a security threat which cuts to the core of agent safety, particularly their families".

He says agents understand the "inherent risks" that come with the job.

"But this incident reportedly includes personal data such as home addresses and contact information, which could expose family members who are normally insulated from the threats associated with such a career," McPherson says.

ShinyHunters shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand.

The samples appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses.

The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.

The criminals also appear to possess highly sensitive medical information relating to thousands of special agents.

BBC News has seen samples of stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations containing information such as blood and urine test results , along with doctors' notes mentioning conditions including a "shellfish and banana allergy".

Agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical issues including "blood in the urine" and "high cholesterol" are now in the criminals' hands.

Cynthia Kaiser, who was the Deputy Director of Cyber at the FBI and now leads the Research Centre at Halcyon says ShinyHunters appear to already have lost control of some of the data which is circulating in various online groups of cyber researchers and could lead to harm even before the main tranche is published.

"A lot of the damage may already be done, and as we have seen in past FBI data breaches, that information continues to circulate the dark web years later," she said.

There are also concerns about the breach's national security implications, such as staff becoming targets for recruitment efforts by hostile foreign intelligence services.

Alongside fear, many of those who spoke to the BBC expressed anger at the FBI for allowing the data to be stolen.

The hack is particularly embarrassing from a technical perspective because ShinyHunters is not generally regarded as a highly sophisticated hacking group.

One former cyber agent said FBI staff were furious about the "sloppy and lazy security failures" that allegedly enabled the breach.

There is also confusion about how to handle any fallout if data is published next week, as threatened.

The FBI appears unlikely to comply with the extortion demands, and the hackers have indicated they intend to post the information on their darknet site.

Unusually, the group is not demanding money. Instead, it wants the FBI to retract an advisory published in May, which it claims "offended" them.

"The agency leadership is lost," the former cyber investigator tells me.

He says staff have been advised to sign up to a service called DeleteMe, which helps remove personal information from data broker websites - a response he feels is inadequate.

According to another former agent, there is widespread shock that such a breach could happen at one of the world's best-resourced law enforcement agencies.

"You would think this information would not be internet-exposed. It's disturbing, actually," he says.

There is also embarrassment that a prolific group of young cyber criminals has repeatedly managed to evade law enforcement while carrying out a string of high-profile hacks.

ShinyHunters has been linked to numerous extortion attacks, including on Rockstar Games and the education platform Canvas .

The group regularly communicates with reporters via Telegram, where members often boast about their activities.

"The bureau doesn't know what to do with teenage cyber criminals," one former agent says.

McPherson says there is no doubt the FBI is taking the incident extremely seriously.

He expects the agency to draw on its extensive network of partners and resources "to make this group suffer the consequences for this brazen and taunting attack".

Kaiser added that the hackers have been "reckless and foolish" and warned them to expect "a significant effort by the FBI to quickly bring them to justice."

items.title: L’Italia digitale dopo i fondi Pnrr: torna A&F Live
items.summary: Lunedì a Milano il talk di Affari&Finanza dedicato all’impatto delle nuove tecnologie sulle imprese e le Pa e alle strategie future. Qui il programma e la registrazione
items.content:
C’è un filo conduttore che attraversa le analisi dello stato dell’Italia digitale: dobbiamo passare dalla realizzazione delle infrastrutture al loro utilizzo. «Creare valore», dicono gli addetti ai lavori nel linguaggio tipico dei manager. Affari&Finanza Live, il talk del settimanale economico di Repubblica, torna lunedì a Milano dal vivo e in diretta streaming. L’obiettivo del convegno, tra riflessioni di docenti, manager e istituzioni, è capire come “Costruire il futuro digitale del Paese”. Un Paese che, emerge dall’analisi degli Osservatori Digital Innovation del Politecnico di Milano sui dati Ue del decennio digitale, ha fatto chiari passi avanti. Rispetto ai target europei al 2030 (tra i relatori ci sarà Roberto Viola, direttore generale della Dg Connect) l’Italia recupera quattro posizioni sull’anno scorso, pur restando 20esima su 27.

Ci sono ambiti in cui siamo sopra la media: tredicesimi per infrastrutture digitali e dodicesimi per trasformazione digitale delle imprese, spiegano i docenti del PoliMi Luca Gastaldi e Andrea Rangone . A spingerci sono l’estensione della copertura 5G sul territorio e gli investimenti in cloud, analisi dei dati e IA, che coinvolgono il 78% delle imprese contro una media europea del 63. In altri aspetti restiamo indietro: ventitreesimo posto per competenze digitali, ventiquattresimo per digitalizzazione dei servizi pubblici. Serve tempo, insistono gli esperti, perché gli investimenti del Pnrr si traducano in miglioramenti effettivi dei servizi.

Abbiamo imparato a prenotare uno screening, pagare una cartella esattoriale, richiedere un bonus governativo attraverso una app pubblica sullo smartphone, ma dagli atti dei processi alla sanità ci sono vasti margini di miglioramento. Ecco quel “creare valore”. Oggi l’89% degli italiani usa regolarmente Internet, contro il 93% della media europea. Ci siamo avvicinati (54%) alla media europea (60%) di cittadini con competenze digitali di base. Il Piano nazionale di ripresa e resilienza ha impresso una fortissima accelerazione: c’è chi arriva a sostenere che senza avremmo atteso un altro ventennio per raggiungere questi livelli. Ma ora che gli investimenti per forza di cose andranno a rallentare, bisogna metterli a frutto.

Molti guardano alla rivoluzione dell’IA come l’abilitatore della creazione di valore dalle infrastrutture fisiche di cui ci siamo dotati. Sempre più centrale nella finanza, come testimoniano alcune grandi banche e assicurazioni, deve ancora affermarsi nel tessuto produttivo tipico della manifattura. Tra le nostre Pmi, il digitale divide: la metà ci investe, l’altra metà è cauta. E sull’IA solo il 15% ha sostenuto spese nel triennio al 2025 , mancando molto spesso delle strategie formalizzate. Un tema centrale, ancor più che digitalizzare le società, è far percepire agli imprenditori la necessità di adeguarsi: molte volte latitano le competenze, a partire dai vertici aziendali.

Per sostenere il suo sviluppo, ad A&F Live si affronta anche il nodo della costruzione dei data center . Nel triennio al 2025 l’Italia ha attirato 7,1 miliardi di investimenti e se ne prospettano 25 fino al 2028. Ma i numeri consolidati sono stati inferiori alle attese, perché le fabbriche di dati iniziano a scontrarsi con un duplice limite: quello delle risorse “naturali” per alimentarli (acqua per raffreddamento e energia), fattore che inizia a scatenare l’opposizione dei territori. E quello di una regolamentazione che ha visto posizionarsi numerosi tasselli (dai processi autorizzativi all’incentivo dei maxi-investimenti) ma non è ancora unitaria a livello nazionale: sarebbe gradita una regia unica, se non un vero e proprio “ministero Digitale” per gestire le nuove infrastrutture, al pari di strade e binari.

"Nel caso in cui gli Stati Uniti commettessero un errore nei confronti dell'Iran, tutte le loro basi operative e i loro interessi nella regione saranno oggetto di attacchi continui, efficaci e dolorosi, senza alcun vincolo o riserva", si legge in una dichiarazione rilasciata oggi dal Quartier Generale Centrale di Khatamolanbiya, riportata dall'agenzia iraniana Mehr. "Qualsiasi decisione degli Stati Uniti di sferrare nuovi attacchi contro l'Iran deve tenere conto del fatto che la regione non è costituita da un unico campo di battaglia; il Golfo Persico, il Mar Rosso, le basi statunitensi e altre località della regione potrebbero tutte essere colpite dalle conseguenze di uno scontro diretto", ha aggiunto. "Le forze armate iraniane sono pronte ad affrontare qualsiasi scenario e qualsiasi errore di valutazione da parte del nemico sarà contrastato con una risposta decisa e massiccia. Qualora le nazioni della regione — persistendo in una politica ambigua nei confronti dell'Iran — si allineassero a un atto di aggressione da parte del 'Grande Satana' (riferendosi agli Stati Uniti), verrebbero tutte considerate complici di questo atto di malvagità e non potrebbero più aspettarsi moderazione o tolleranza da parte delle potenti forze armate iraniane" ha concluso il Quartier Generale Centrale di Khatamolanbiya

Al via le candidature in vista delle attese elezioni palestinesi di novembre. La commissione elettorale centrale dell'Autorità palestinese ha reso noto che è aperta la procedura per la presentazione delle candidature a due mesi dal voto previsto per il 28 novembre. C'è tempo fino al 7 ottobre, riferisce l'agenzia palestinese Wafa, per la presentazione delle liste negli uffici centrali di al-Birej, in Cisgiordania, e Deir al-Balah, nella Striscia di Gaza. La comunità internazionale teme un rinvio del voto, in particolare per problemi logistici. Risalgono al 2006 le ultime elezioni legislative nei Territori palestinesi. Era l'anno del trionfo di Hamas su Fatah, il partito del leader dell'Anp, Mahmoud Abbas, 91 anni a novembre. Dal 2007, anno in cui Hamas prese il controllo della Striscia di Gaza, il Consiglio legislativo palestinese, il Parlamento dell'Anp, non si riunisce in sessione ordinaria. A luglio Abbas, vincitore delle ultime elezioni per la presidenza dell'Anp del 2005, ha annunciato la data del voto per le legislative. Non è chiaro, evidenziano i media israeliani, se Hamas o candidati affiliati potranno partecipare alle elezioni. Non c'è ancora una data per le presidenziali che dovrebbero tenersi nel primo trimestre del prossimo anno

Mauritius, negato il permesso di atterraggio a un volo da Israele: “Decisione politica”

Secondo l'agenzia di viaggi Spirit World Productions, un volo Air Seychelles è stato cancellato dopo che Mauritius ha vietato l'atterraggio a un volo proveniente da Israele. La compagnia ha affermato che il volo è stato cancellato "nonostante gli sforzi compiuti durante la notte e, secondo le informazioni fornite, si è trattato di una decisione dettata da considerazioni politiche"

Trump pubblica su Truth la mappa nella quale Hormuz diventa lo “Stretto di Trump”

Lo "Stretto di Trump". Nella notte Donald Trump ha pubblicato su Truth una mappa in cui lo Stretto di Hormuz viene indicato come "Stretto di Trump". Nei giorni scorsi, affermando che "stiamo vincendo la guerra" e "controlliamo lo Stretto di Hormuz", il tycoon ribadiva che "dovremmo chiamarlo 'Stretto di Trump'". "Dovrò pur ricavarci qualcosa", aggiungeva. Ad agosto il tycoon aveva pubblicato su Truth un'immagine con una mappa dello Stretto di Hormuz descritto "nuovo Territorio Usa"

President Trump posts the renamed Strait of Hormuz to the "Trump Strait", since the U.S. Military has 100% control. Oil is flowing and broke a 6 month record. pic.twitter.com/05B7YhehDx

Media: “Intelligence egiziana avvertì Israele prima del 7 ottobre”

Abbas Kamel, capo dell'intelligence egiziana, si era recato in Israele il 26 settembre 2023 per avvertire che Hamas sembrava prepararsi a un attacco su larga scala e il tempo utile per scongiurare un disastro stava per scadere. Lo riporta The Atlantic, citando funzionari israeliani, egiziani, statunitensi ed europei. Kamel non fornì ai funzionari israeliani una data, né informazioni specifiche su quello che meno di due settimane dopo, il 7 ottobre, si sarebbe rivelato un attacco multidimensionale contro Israele, e non è chiaro con chi esattamente abbia avuto colloqui, specifica The Atlantic, ma secondo un ex funzionario israeliano "non esiste scenario possibile" in cui i vertici israeliani incontrino il capo dell'intelligence egiziana senza che il primo ministro Benjamin Netanyahu "ne sia al corrente". Nei giorni successivi all'attacco, l'ufficio di Netanyahu ha negato che il premier avesse ricevuto avvertimenti dall'Egitto riguardo alla situazione a Gaza

"Non ha alcun problema di salute particolare né difficoltà in corso". Ha risposto così il presidente iraniano, Masoud Pezeshkian, a una domanda della Cbs sulla Guida Suprema dell'Iran, Mojtaba Khamenei, che non si è mai fatto vedere in pubblico da quando, a inizio marzo, ha preso il posto del padre, Ali Khamenei, ucciso all'inizio delle operazioni militari che il 28 febbraio scorso Usa e Israele avviarono contro l'Iran. In un'intervista Pezeshkian, cardiochirurgo, ha affermato di aver incontrato in "due occasioni" Mojtaba Khamenei e ha sottolineato come l'ultimo faccia a faccia sia andato avanti per "oltre sette "ore. "Dal punto di vista clinico, è in perfetta salute - ha ripetuto - Ascoltatemi, ascoltatemi come medico. Non ha alcun problema di salute".

Pezeshkian: “Gli ispettori nucleari dell’Onu potranno entrare in Iran”

In un'intervista a Cbs News Pezeshkian ha affermato che l'Iran potrebbe consentire il ritorno degli ispettori nucleari dell'Onu. Quando gli è stato chiesto delle precedenti restrizioni imposte agli ispettori dell'Agenzia internazionale per l'energia atomica (Aiea) delle Nazioni Unite e se ora sarebbe stato loro consentito l'accesso, ha risposto che la dichiarazione era "corretta", aggiungendo: "Se desiderano entrare ed effettuare ispezioni, possiamo raggiungere accordi e intese su questo specifico argomento nell'ambito dei negoziati".

La coalizione a guida saudita ha annunciato di aver intercettato e distrutto due droni diretti verso Riad e due missili balistici lanciati dagli Houthi contro Khamis Mushait, città nel sudovest dell'Arabia Saudita che ospita una base aerea. I nuovi attacchi del gruppo yemenita sostenuto dall'Iran arrivano dopo la condanna del Consiglio di sicurezza dell'Onu per l'escalation contro il regno.

Media: “Trump ha respinto la proposta di accordo, nuovi attacchi dopo le elezioni di midterm”

Donald Trump ha respinto il piano iraniano per un tregua di sette giorni a ha riferito ai suoi collaboratori che intende riprendere a bombardare l'Iran dopo le elezioni di metà mandato. Lo riporta il Wall Street Journal citando alcune fonti, secondo il quale la proposta iraniana avrebbe portato alla riapertura dello Stretto di Hormuz e alla ripresa dei negoziati sul nucleare, in cambio della revoca del blocco americano.

In un'intervista a CBS News , Pezzeskian ha affermato che "se gli Stati Uniti accetteranno la proposta dell’Iran di sette giorni riguardo allo Stretto di Hormuz, il processo di attuazione inizierà immediatamente e le forze militari del governo iraniano vi aderiranno". Il presidente iraniano ha esaminato questa proposta nel quadro del Memorandum d'intesa di Islamabad, che persegue gli stessi obiettivi, e ha affermato: "In definitiva, le richieste incluse in quel memorandum e in quell'intesa sono state ora suddivise in fasi, in modo da poter procedere in base a tali fasi".

Dopo la notizia diffusa da Haaretz su un presunto avvertimento a Benjamin Netanyahu da parte del presidente degli Emirati Arabi Uniti, Mohammed bin Zayed, sull'attacco del 7 ottobre, una nuova inchiesta giornalistica potrebbe alimentare il caos in Israele. Secondo la rivista The Atlantic , poco prima dell'invasione giuidata da Hamas, un avvertimento egiziano fu trasmesso dall'allora capo dell'intelligence egiziana, Abbas Kamel, ad alti funzionari israeliani all'aeroporto Ben Gurion. Già due giorni dopo la strage messa in atto dall'organizzazione palestinese, un funzionario dell'intelligence egiziana aveva dichiarato all' Associated Press che Israele aveva ignorato ripetuti avvertimenti sul fatto che Hamas stesse pianificando "qualcosa di grosso", e il sito di notizie Ynet aveva riferito che proprio Kamel aveva avvertito personalmente Netanyahu dieci giorni prima delle atrocità.

items.title: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
items.summary: Climate change is transforming Papua's snowy peaks, which hold scientific value and spiritual significance.
items.content:
The mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries.

The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.

They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.

A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.

But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.

Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime.

"There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".

She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.

Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history.

Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.

But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.

The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.

As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.

El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.

The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.

A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.

The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".

At least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations.

The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow".

"Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity."

According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live.

Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts.

"How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed."

For many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event.

The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape.

Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys.

Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded.

The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment.

"Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people."

As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left.

Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains.

From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts."

Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change.

"When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains.

Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed.

"I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation."

items.content:
Stati Uniti e Russia hanno fatto fronte comune per impedire l'introduzione di limiti all'impiego dell'intelligenza artificiale nei sistemi d'arma. Lo ha rivelato il Washington Post . Tra le proposte bloccate, l'obbligo che a prendere la decisione finale su quali obbiettivi colpire tra quelli suggeriti dall'intelligenza artificiale sia un essere umano e non un computer.

A Kiev e Kharkiv scatta l’allarme droni mentre Dmitriev , rappresentante di Putin per la cooperazione economica, si trova a New York per una serie di colloqui. I droni ucraini hanno colpito una raffineria nella regione russa del Krasnodar. Indagini sull’incidente che ha coinvolto quattro militari italiani durante un addestramento Nato in Lettonia

Media: “Usa e Russia bloccano le limitazioni all’uso dell’Ia negli armamenti”

Stati Uniti e Russia hanno fatto fronte comune per impedire l'introduzione di limiti all'impiego dell'intelligenza artificiale nei sistemi d'arma. Lo ha rivelato il Washington Post. Tra le proposte bloccate, l'obbligo che a prendere la decisione finale su quali obiettivi colpire tra quelli suggeriti dall'intelligenza artificiale sia un essere umano e non un computer. Il quotidiano americano ha raccontato il dietro le quinte della riunione del Gruppo di esperti governativi sui sistemi d'arma autonomi letali (Laws), nell'ambito della convenzione delle Nazioni Unite alcune armi convenzionali (Ccw) che si è tenuta a Ginevra all'inizio di settembre. Centinaia di diplomatici si sono incontrati in Svizzera per lavorare a un trattato per regolamentare l'uso delle armi autonome letali basati sull'intelligenza artificiale. L'ultimo giorno dei negoziati, la discussione ha assunto toni particolarmente accesi, ha spiegato Wp. Nelle 15 ore successive, diplomatici statunitensi e russi hanno lavorato intensamente sul testo del documento per eliminare una serie di disposizioni concepite per introdurre garanzie e limiti nell'utilizzo dell'Ia. Nella versione finale del testo, sono saltate le diverse misure di salvaguardia che alcuni Paesi e organizzazioni avevano proposto per ridurre i rischi associati all'impiego di sistemi d'arma autonomi controllati dall'Ia. Secondo le fonti, sono state eliminate le formulazioni che imponevano ai sistemi di operare o in modo "prevedibile" e "affidabile", ed è stata rimossa anche una clausola che richiedeva di tenere conto delle considerazioni etiche nell'impiego di armamenti basati sull'intelligenza artificiale. Le delegazioni di Stati Uniti e Russia hanno inoltre eliminato una disposizione che imponeva una revisione "umana" degli obiettivi militari individuati dall'Ia prima di un attacco Washington e Mosca erano arrivate a Ginevra attrezzate per l'offensiva: entrambe le delegazioni comprendevano una decina di giuristi, quasi il doppio delle altre, pronti a dare battaglia sulle virgole. Il gruppo americano era composto da rappresentati del dipartimento di Stato e del Pentagono, oltre che avvocati. Al momento i negoziati sono ancora in fase preliminare. A novembre a Ginevra gli stati membri dell'Onu decideranno se procedere verso un trattato vincolante. Ma anche se la maggioranza dei paesi dovesse votare a favore, difficilmente un testo garantista potrà vedere la luce. Stati Uniti e Russia sono ormai sempre meno sostenitori del multilateralismo e possono usare "il loro capitale politico per esercitare pressioni su altri Paesi", ha avvertito Nicole van Rooijen, direttore esecutivo della coalizione non governativa globale Stop Killer Robots

Putin aprirà la Duma il 30 settembre: proteste per presunti brogli

Vladimir Putin presiederà il 30 settembre la prima seduta della nuova Duma, eletta nelle contestate legislative del 18-20 settembre, mentre l'opposizione avvia proteste per denunciare presunti brogli. Lo ha annunciato Viktor Pinski, responsabile del gruppo di lavoro incaricato di preparare l'apertura della nona legislatura della Camera bassa russa, dove Russia Unita, il partito del Cremlino, disporrà nuovamente della maggioranza costituzionale. La formazione di governo ha ottenuto 349 dei 450 seggi. Putin ha difeso il risultato, sostenendo che i russi abbiano votato in maggioranza per la vittoria dell'esercito in Ucraina. "Voglio rivolgermi ai nostri soldati e comandanti al fronte. Voglio che sappiate, compagni, che questo voto è per voi. La gente crede in voi, nella nostra vittoria, nel vostro eroismo e nella vostra lealtà alla patria", ha dichiarato questa settimana. L'annuncio della seduta inaugurale coincide con la mobilitazione dell'opposizione, che denuncia la falsificazione dei risultati sia nel voto di lista sia nei collegi elettorali. Russia Unita è risultata vincitrice in tutte le regioni del Paese. La prima manifestazione si è svolta ieri a Syktyvkar, capitale della repubblica dei Komi, su iniziativa del Partito comunista. Vi hanno partecipato circa cento persone, dopo che l'amministrazione comunale non aveva nè autorizzato nè vietato l'iniziativa. Proteste analoghe sono state convocate in altre dieci città della Russia europea e della Siberia, tra cui Mosca, San Pietroburgo, Kazan ed Ekaterinburg. In alcuni casi le autorità locali hanno respinto formalmente le richieste

Un attacco russo alla città ucraina di Sumy ha causato la morte di due persone. Lo hanno riferito le autorità locali

Cremlino: “Telefonata Putin-Vucic, focus su energia, petrolio e gas”

Il presidente russo Vladimir Putin ha discusso al telefono con il presidente serbo Aleksandar Vucic diversi aspetti dell'ulteriore sviluppo del partenariato strategico tra Russia e Serbia, anche nei settori dell'energia, del petrolio e del gas. Lo riferisce il Cremlino, citato dall'agenzia Interfax

Kiev: “La popolazione della città occupata di Oleshky sta morendo di fame”

"La popolazione di Oleshky, città temporaneamente occupata, sta morendo di fame. Non è rimasto quasi più nulla da mangiare". È quanto scrive sui social il ministro degli Esteri ucraino Andrii Sybiha. "Secondo quanto riferito, i civili sono costretti a sopravvivere nutrendosi di erba e erbacce, mentre medicinali, acqua potabile, elettricità e assistenza sanitaria sono sempre più irraggiungibili. Anche i bambini sono intrappolati in queste condizioni", aggiunge Sybiha, "questa sofferenza ha una causa chiara e un responsabile ben preciso. La Russia ha provocato questa catastrofe a Oleshky con la sua occupazione illegale e si assume la piena responsabilità di questo disastro umanitario, di tutte le sue conseguenze e delle vite di civili innocenti perse a causa di esso"

Le forze ucraine hanno attaccato nella notte la raffineria di Ilski, nella regione russa di Krasnodar, provocando un incendio all'interno dell'impianto. Lo ha riferito lo Stato maggiore delle forze armate ucraine in un comunicato pubblicato su Telegram. La raffineria ha una capacità di lavorazione di circa 6,6 milioni di tonnellate di petrolio all'anno. Secondo lo Stato maggiore, l'impianto riceve, immagazzina e raffina materie prime a base di idrocarburi, oltre a produrre e distribuire derivati petroliferi. La produzione, ha aggiunto Kiev, viene utilizzata anche per soddisfare le esigenze delle forze armate russe

Zelensky: “Escalation russa quotidiana, nella notte 2 morti e 14 feriti”

"Solo questa notte, 14 persone sono rimaste ferite a causa degli attacchi russi. Sono stati sferrati numerosi attacchi contro edifici residenziali a Kiev, Zaporizhzhia, nelle regioni di Odessa, Sumy e Kharkiv. Purtroppo, due persone hanno perso la vita a Zaporizhzhia". È quanto scrive sui social il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky. "Le mie condoglianze ai familiari e ai cari. Si registrano danni alle infrastrutture civili: un asilo nido a Kiev, un liceo nella regione di Kiev, un'università a Kharkiv, impianti energetici nelle regioni di Poltava, Mykolaiv e Vinnytsia", aggiunge, "è importante che i nostri partner non dimentichino che l'escalation russa si verifica ogni giorno". "Se i russi hanno scelto di rendere i loro attacchi ancora più brutali, il mondo deve scegliere risposte più forti per impedire che la guerra si estenda ulteriormente", si legge ancora nel post, "chiediamo al presidente Trump di applicare la legge di Lindsey Graham contro la Russia e tutti coloro che sostengono finanziariamente la sua guerra. Chiediamo ai presidenti António Costa e Ursula von der Leyen di introdurre ulteriori sanzioni europee. Chiediamo a tutti i leader di non escludere gli oligarchi russi dalle attuali liste di sanzioni e di continuare a limitare qualsiasi commercio con i terroristi finché la Russia non metterà fine alla guerra. È proprio così, con sforzi comuni quotidiani, che la pace deve avvicinarsi".

Un centro di elaborazione dati di Starlink è stato colpito nella notte in un attacco su Kiev. Lo riferisce l'agenzia russa Tass, citando il ministero della Difesa di Mosca. La struttura colpita si troverebbe a Kosmonova, indicata nei resoconti russi come un sobborgo di Kiev, e avrebbe fornito supporto all'esercito ucraino. Già ieri sera era stato attaccato un altro centro dati, appartenente a Datagroup. Secondo le ricostruzioni russe, l'edificio avrebbe rappresentato un nodo centrale per l'elaborazione e la trasmissione di informazioni dell'intelligence ucraina.

items.title: Russia targeting 'ordinary life' with attacks on Ukraine's data centres, Zelensky says
items.summary: Such strikes aim to disrupt "people's ability to stay connected, study, work", says Ukraine's president.
items.content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia has widened its attacks to target Ukraine's data centres and internet providers, seeking to cause maximum disruption for ordinary people.

"All this affects people's ability to stay connected, study, work," he said.

On Friday a Russian drone hit a business centre in the capital Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. A separate attack killed a 14-year-old boy. Israel's foreign ministry said he was an Israeli citizen.

Russia confirmed it had targeted a data centre site, saying it was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence.

About 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages on Wednesday due to strikes.

Some firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.

In the north-western city of Lutsk, electronic information boards at public transport stops were not working on Friday, officials said. The city council said this was "due to damage caused by a Russian attack on data centres in Kyiv".

In Friday's social media post, Zelensky wrote: "The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centres, internet providers – for Russia, all ordinary life is simply a target.

"It is important that the world responds to all of this and that Russia feels the response to its terror."

Late on Friday, Zelensky said "additional decisions" had been made at his meeting with Ukraine's top defence and security officials to protect the country's data centres and other critical communications facilities to ensure their continuous operation.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said that Russia was seeking to disrupt the flow of "life-saving information" by targeting data centres.

"Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential - they save lives. This is critical civilian infrastructure... It is not a military target. It is essential to keeping everyday life functioning," Sybiha said.

Zelensky's top adviser on defence technologies on Thursday admitted that "there may be local disruptions" following Russian attacks an the cost of internet services could increase to cover the costs of repairs.

But Serhii Beskrestnov stressed that Ukraine's internet network was highly decentralised, so the country "will not be left without internet access".

The data centre hit by Russia on Friday was run by Datagroup. The company said its specialists were assessing the damage after the daytime attack but all services "continue to operate from backup sites".

Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said on Friday evening that seven people had been killed and 59 injured after Russian overnight attacks.

Russia's defence ministry later confirmed it had hit the Datagroup site, which it said was being used by the Ukrainian military's intelligence.

Footage showing the damaged Inkom business centre that housed Datagroup has since been verified by the BBC.

The Russian defence ministry also said that over the past few days its forces have targeted a number of data processing and telecommunications centres in Ukraine, including New-Telco, United DC, Kyivstar and Parkovyi.

In recent weeks, Moscow has also intensified its strikes on Ukraine's energy and railway infrastructure – seeking to cause maximum damage as winter approaches.

Ukraine's military has been hitting Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, saying they help finance Russia's ongoing war effort.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water

Russia's elections had few surprises - but how the Kremlin uses the results will be crucial

Speaking to reporters late on Friday, Putin said Moscow would "give careful thought" to the idea of resuming direct peace negotiations with Kyiv, citing last week's "massive" Ukrainian attack on the capital Moscow and other recent strikes.

"It's all possible," he said, but stressed that Ukraine "must feel our retaliatory strikes", and that all decisions would be taken "based on the Russian Federation's interests".

Zelensky had earlier said he was ready for trilateral talks that would also involve the US.

Kyiv and its European allies have repeatedly accused Putin of rejecting any peace negotiations, saying he was seeking to seize more Ukrainian territory.

Speaking to the media, Putin also restated his position that Moscow had "no plans" and "no reason" to attack Europe. He had made similar statements about Ukraine, before launching his full-scale invasion almost five years ago.

In a separate development on Friday, the European Union agreed to release €6.6bn for Ukraine, the bloc's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said, describing this as "good news for Ukraine and bad news for Russia".

This includes €900 million for the EU's Military Assistance Mission for Ukraine, and a €1 billion fund for joint procurement of equipment, she said on X.

"Moscow's hybrid attacks try to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine. Europe is doing the opposite."

Meanwhile, Poland's prosecutors opened an investigation in what they said was an arson attack on a Starlink satellite station in Wola Krobowska on Wednesday.

In a statement, the national prosecutor's office said "there is a reasonable suspicion... that the perpetrators acted on the orders of the Russian special services". Moscow has not commented.

The station transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals.

In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have warned Russia may be preparing hybrid attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies.

Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport , while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites .
